Sample text:
---
# A Temporary Arrangement

There is a moment during a total solar eclipse, in the last seconds before totality, when the light goes strange. Not dark—not yet—but thin, silvered, the color of the inside of a shell. Shadows sharpen. The air cools. Birds, confused, head for their roosts, and a strange stillness falls, as if the world were holding its breath. Then the last bead of sunlight slips behind the Moon, and the corona blooms into view: a pearly halo of ionized gas, two million degrees, invisible at every other moment of your life.

You can only see it because of a coincidence.

The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon. It is also, at this moment in the history of the solar system, about four hundred times farther away. The two discs therefore appear the same size in our sky—a match so exact that the Moon can slide across the face of the Sun and extinguish it completely, leaving only the corona burning around a black hole where noon used to be. The match is not perfect. Both orbits are ellipses, so sometimes the Moon is a little too far and you get a ring of fire instead. But it is close enough that total and annular eclipses still alternate, and nothing in the physics requires even that.

The Moon is leaving.

Not dramatically. It drifts away at about 3.8 centimeters per year—the speed at which your fingernails grow—measured by bouncing lasers off the reflectors Apollo left on the surface. The cause is tides. The Moon's gravity raises bulges in Earth's oceans; Earth's rotation drags those bulges slightly ahead of the Moon; the bulges tug the Moon forward in its orbit, and slowly, patiently, the Moon gains energy and climbs to a higher orbit. The exchange is mutual. Earth slows. Our days are lengthening by roughly two milliseconds every century. The torque is tiny. The accumulated effect, over geological time, is not.

Go back far enough and the days were shorter. Corals from the Devonian, 370 million years ago, laid down growth bands like tree rings; count them and you find roughly 400 days in the year—days of about twenty-two hours. Wind further back, to the giant impact that formed the Moon 4.5 billion years ago—a Mars-sized body striking the young Earth and spinning a ring of molten debris into orbit—and the day may have lasted four or five hours. The Moon, newly born and hanging low and enormous in that primordial sky, would have dominated the heavens. It has been rising, and retreating, ever since.

This means the dinosaurs lived under a different Moon. It means the armies of Lydia and Media, who supposedly stopped a war in 585 BC because Thales had forecast the darkness, stood on a day when the match of apparent sizes was a shade more precise than it is now. Total eclipses were slightly more total.

And it means that the match is running down.

Because the Moon recedes, its apparent size shrinks. Because the Sun slowly brightens and swells as it ages, the Sun's apparent size grows. The two discs are drifting apart in the sky, and around 600 million years from now, by most calculations, the Moon will no longer be able to cover the Sun completely. Totality will be gone. Every eclipse will be annular—a ring of fire, the corona drowned in sunlight, the strange silver dark a thing of the past. The golden age of total solar eclipses, a few hundred million years bracketed by irrelevance, will close. No mark will be left. There may be no one left to notice: in roughly a billion years, a brightening Sun is expected to make the oceans unreliable, and complex life may be a memory.

Even now, the arrangement is exclusive. Any given spot on Earth sees a total eclipse about once every 375 years, and the Moon's umbra—the small dark footprint of totality, rarely more than 270 kilometers across—sweeps across the planet like a searchlight, missing almost everyone. You have to be in the one place, at the one time. Totality itself lasts minutes. The longest possible, near the equator, around seven and a half.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable. There is something in the eclipse that condenses a truth about almost everything: that the configurations we take as permanent are temporary alignments, arrived at by drift, that will not hold. The Moon and Sun are not collaborating. Nobody arranged the match. It is a crossing of two unrelated ratios, and we happen to be alive during the crossing. The same is true of the temperature of the oceans, the chemistry of the air, the tilt of the Earth's axis—which the Moon helps to steady, keeping the seasons from wandering. We live inside a braid of coincidences that we did not tie and cannot keep.

Which is not, I think, a reason for melancholy. It is a reason for attention. The universe is mostly like this—states that hold for a while, and then don't. The eclipse is just unusually legible about it. You can stand in the shadow of the Moon, in that small dark room the size of a city moving across the land at the speed of a jet, and feel the coincidence in your body: the sudden cold, the corona, the horizon glowing sunset-red all around, because somewhere outside the umbra it is still noon. For two or three minutes you are standing in a place where the arithmetic of the sky has come briefly true. Then the diamond ring flashes, daylight slams back on, and the alignment moves on without you.

The Moon will keep leaving, a fingernail's growth per year. Long after the eclipses have failed, long after anything that could be nostalgic about them is gone, it will still be receding—unless the Sun, dying, swells first and puts an end to the whole arrangement. Either way, the meeting that made totality possible was never a promise. It was a window. We are in it. The corona is visible. That is not nothing.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical science essay turns the changing geometry of an eclipse into a meditation on impermanence and attention.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient and image-rich, moving from precise astronomical explanation toward personal reflection without abandoning the science. Its pathos comes from the mismatch between the eclipse’s extraordinary beauty and its temporary, accidental nature. The speaker explicitly resists melancholy, inviting the reader instead to notice the rare alignment while it lasts.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds cosmic coincidence, slow change, and the limits of permanence: the receding Moon, lengthening days, and the eventual end of total eclipses. It pairs measurable details—laser reflectors, orbital drift, geological time—with sensory images of cold air, silvered light, and the corona. Its moral emphasis is attention to a temporary window, not grief over its closing.

## Evidence line
> We live inside a braid of coincidences that we did not tie and cannot keep.

Medium: the sample is coherent and stylistically distinctive, with its scientific detail repeatedly serving a clear emphasis on impermanence and attention.
